title: ‘We praise God’: Australian woman feared missing in Nepal flooding makes contact with family - The Guardian
description: ‘We praise God’: Australian woman feared missing in Nepal flooding makes contact with family  The Guardian
publisher.title: The Guardian
full_article:
An Australian woman has made contact with her family, more than two days after she was reported missing in flash flooding in Nepal.

At least 584 people have been killed and more than 1,900 are missing after a catastrophic flash flood hit the China-Nepal border on Wednesday. Cara Severino, 25, is the first of 39 Australians reported missing in the tragedy to have been confirmed safe.

Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email

But she is still hiking away from the disaster zone, attempting to reach Kathmandu on foot with a group of Nepali hikers – a trek of more than 110km.

Her parents, Debbie and Frank Severino, confirmed in a statement that she had no phone reception, and her own phone had a flat battery, but that she had contacted them on Friday morning to say she was safe.

“She was hiking the Langtang trek and was stranded,” they said in a statement. “With communications down we had no contact.”

2:02 Timeline of how deadly Nepal and Tibet flash flood unfolded – explainer

“This morning she was able to call us from Gosainkunda where she has been able to reach along with some other [Nepali] hikers. We understand that they are attempting to reach Kathmandu on foot.

“We eagerly await more information about her safe return. We praise God that she has been able to make this brief contact with us. Our thoughts and prayers are with all the families awaiting news.”

As of Friday evening, 38 Australians were missing. Of the 35 missing Australians whose details were released by Nepali police, Severino was the only one not listed as travelling with a tour agency.

The others were from four other groups, many of them organised to take part in the Mount Kailash Hindu pilgrimage in the region.

title: ‘Immense impact’ of Nepal flood disaster highlighted as casualties mount - UN News
description: ‘Immense impact’ of Nepal flood disaster highlighted as casualties mount  UN News
publisher.title: UN News
full_article:
The catastrophic flooding occurred at the border between Nepal and the Tibet autonomous region of China.

It is thought to have been caused by the collapse of a glacier and the resulting landslide, leading to the destruction of entire communities as well as key infrastructure including bridges and roads.

On Friday, quoting Government of Nepal figures the UN’s aid coordination office OCHA said that 538 people had died, while almost 3,750 had been rescued. Around 1000 people are still missing, many of whom are thought to be tourists.

The Tibet autonomous region of China was also affected and some 560 people remain missing there, according to the authorities.

Tweet URL

Lila Pieters Yahia, the UN Resident Coordinator in Nepal who visited the disaster zone said the search and rescue effort was ongoing.

“We witnessed people had just been rescued as we were walking and visiting the site, one of the sites which has been severely damaged,” she said. “We saw a whole truck full of people, an entire family had just been rescued and I can tell you it was very, very emotional.”

Her visit was cut short after a renewed flood alert was issued.

Relief effort

Aid teams have been working around the clock to reach communities cut off by the disaster in the Nepalese districts of Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading.

© UNICEF/Robic Upadhayay Emergency supplies are prepared for delivery to flood-affected communities in Nepal.

The UN is supporting the relief effort with emergency food rations, medical kits for about 10,000 people for three months, as well as tents and logistics support. It is also providing satellite imagery and analysis of the area affected by the flood.

Meanwhile, the World Health Organization (WHO) has warned of the risk of disease. “As always, when we have disaster of this scale and we have displacement, overcrowding, and we may have disruption of water, sanitation and health services, and that can increase the risk of infectious diseases,” said spokesperson Tarik Jašarević in Geneva.

UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) spokesperson Ricardo Pires told reporters that while 18 schools have been completely destroyed and another 20 have been damaged, “dozens more are located close to the riverbanks and remain at high risk,” meaning an estimated 10,000 school-aged children in the area need support to continue their education.

Disaster-affected region

The area was hit by a 7.8 magnitude earthquake in April 2015, which killed more than 8,800 people.

Last October, torrential rains caused fast-moving floods and landslides across eastern and central Nepal, affecting more than 30,000 people.

Kamal Kishore, the Head of the UN Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) highlighted the seriousness of the disaster. “In living memory, we haven't seen a mountain hazard event like this for a very, very long time,” he said, adding that “the impact on lives, livelihoods, buildings, infrastructure, bridges, hydroelectric projects, power generation, it's really immense. And I think we are still coming to grips with the extent of the damage.”

He added that the current situation is marked by “extremely high risk as well as a lot of uncertainty.”

“It's a unique challenge for the emergency response itself, because in a sense, the disaster is not yet completely over,” he stressed.

The floods have “again highlighted how fragile mountain ecosystems are and how challenging it is to set up early warning systems in mountain environments,” focusing on a range of cascading hazards.

The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) which is working alongside the UN in Nepal said it was “very, very concerned about the secondary flood.”

The IFRC believes that at least 93,000 people have been affected and are “in great need.”

नेपाल आ चीन के तिब्बत स्वायत्त क्षेत्र के सीमा पर विनाशकारी बाढ़ि आयल अछि।

मानलऽ जाय छै कि एकरऽ कारण ग्लेशियर केरऽ ढहला आरू एकरऽ परिणामस्वरूप भूस्खलन होय ​​गेलऽ छै, जेकरा चलतें पूरा समुदाय के साथ-साथ पुल आरू सड़क सहित प्रमुख बुनियादी ढाँचा के भी नष्ट होय गेलऽ छै ।

शुक्रदिन नेपाल सरकार के आंकड़ा के हवाला दैत संयुक्त राष्ट्र के सहायता समन्वय कार्यालय ओसीएचए कहलनि जे, 538 लोक के मौत भ गेल अछि, जखन कि लगभग 3,750 के बचाओल गेल अछि। करीब 1000 लोक एखनो लापता छथि, जाहि मे सं बहुतो के पर्यटक मानल जाइत अछि.

चीन केरऽ तिब्बत स्वायत्त क्षेत्र भी प्रभावित होय गेलै आरू वहाँ लगभग ५६० लोग लापता छै, अधिकारियऽ के अनुसार ।

ट्वीट यूआरएल

आपदा क्षेत्रमे गेल नेपालमे संयुक्त राष्ट्रसंघके निवासी समन्वयक लीला पीटर्स याहिया खोज आ बचाव प्रयास जारी रहल बतौलनि ।

ओ कहली जे हम सब देखलहुं जे एखनहि लोक कए बचाउल गेल छल, जखन हम सब पैदल चलैत छलहुं आ एहि स्थल पर जा रहल छलहुं, जे ओहि स्थल मे स एक अछि जे काफी क्षतिग्रस्त भ गेल अछि। “हमरा लोकनि एकटा पूरा ट्रक लोक सँ भरल देखलहुँ, एकटा पूरा परिवार केँ एखनहि बचाओल गेल छल आ हम अहाँ केँ कहि सकैत छी जे ई बहुत, बहुत भावुक छल।”

नयका बाढ़ अलर्ट जारी भेलाक बाद हुनकर यात्रा कम भ गेल।

राहत प्रयास

नेपालक रसुवा, नुवाकोट आ धादिङ जिल्लामे आपदासँ कटल समुदाय तक पहुँचबामे सहायता दल चौबीसों घंटा कार्यरत रहल अछि ।

© यूनिसेफ/रोबिक उपाध्याय नेपाल मे बाढ़ि प्रभावित समुदाय मे आपातकालीन सामान पहुँचेबाक लेल तैयार कएल गेल अछि ।

संयुक्त राष्ट्र आपातकालीन भोजन राशन, तीन महीना तक लगभग 10,000 लोगऽ लेली मेडिकल किट के साथ-साथ टेंट आरू रसद सहायता के साथ राहत प्रयास के समर्थन करी रहलऽ छै । संगहि बाढ़ि सं प्रभावित इलाका के उपग्रह इमेजरी आओर विश्लेषण सेहो द रहल अछि.

एम्हर विश्व स्वास्थ्य संगठन (डब्ल्यूएचओ) बीमारी के खतरा के चेतावनी देलक अछि। जेनेवा मँ प्रवक्ता तारिक जाशारेविच नँ कहलकै, “हमेशा के तरह, जबे हमरा सब के पास ई पैमाना के आपदा आबै छै आरू हमरा सब के पास विस्थापन, भीड़भाड़ छै, आरू हमरा पास पानी, स्वच्छता आरू स्वास्थ्य सेवा मँ बाधा आबी सकै छै, आरू जेकरा स॑ संक्रामक बीमारी के खतरा बढ़ी सकै छै ।

संयुक्त राष्ट्र बाल कोष (यूनिसेफ) केरऽ प्रवक्ता रिकार्डो पाइरेस न॑ पत्रकारऽ स॑ कहलकै कि जहां १८ स्कूल पूरा तरह स॑ नष्ट होय गेलऽ छै आरू २० आरू क्षतिग्रस्त होय गेलऽ छै, वहीं “दर्जनों आरू स्कूल नदी के किनारे के नजदीक स्थित छै आरू उच्च जोखिम म॑ छै,” मतलब कि ई क्षेत्र केरऽ लगभग १०,००० स्कूली उम्र के बच्चा सिनी क॑ अपनऽ शिक्षा जारी रखै लेली सहायता के जरूरत छै ।

आपदा प्रभावित क्षेत्र

ई क्षेत्र म॑ अप्रैल २०१५ म॑ ७.८ तीव्रता के भूकंप आबी गेलऽ छेलै, जेकरा म॑ ८,८०० स॑ भी अधिक लोगऽ के मौत होय गेलऽ छेलै ।

पिछला अक्टूबर मे मूसलाधार वर्षा के कारण पूर्वी आ मध्य नेपाल मे तेजी सं बाढ़ि आ भूस्खलन भेल छल जाहि सं 30 हजार सं बेसि लोक प्रभावित भेल छल.

संयुक्त राष्ट्र आपदा जोखिम कम करय के कार्यालय (यूएनडीआरआर) के प्रमुख कमल किशोर आपदा के गंभीरता पर प्रकाश डाललखिन्ह. ओ कहलनि जे, जीवित स्मृति मे हम सब बहुत, बहुत लंबा समय स एहि तरहक पहाड़ी खतरा क घटना नहि देखलहुं अछि, आ इहो कहलनि जे, “जीवन, आजीविका, भवन, बुनियादी ढांचा, पुल, जलविद्युत परियोजना, बिजली उत्पादन पर एकर असर सचमुच अपार अछि।आ हमरा लगैत अछि जे हम सब एखनो नुकसान क हद पर काबू पाबि रहल छी।”

हुनी आरू कहलकै कि वर्तमान स्थिति म॑ “अत्यंत उच्च जोखिम के साथ-साथ बहुत अनिश्चितता भी छै ।”

हुनी जोर देलकै कि आपातकालीन प्रतिक्रिया लेली ही ई एगो अनूठा चुनौती छै, कैन्हेंकि एक तरह स॑ ई आपदा अभी पूरा तरह स॑ खत्म नै होय सकलऽ छै ।

बाढ़ न॑ “फिर स॑ ई बात प॑ प्रकाश डाललकै कि पहाड़ी पारिस्थितिकी तंत्र कतेक नाजुक छै आरू पहाड़ी वातावरण म॑ जल्दी चेतावनी प्रणाली स्थापित करना कतेक चुनौतीपूर्ण छै,” जेकरा म॑ झरना के खतरा के एक श्रृंखला प॑ ध्यान देलऽ गेलऽ छै ।

नेपालमे संयुक्त राष्ट्र संघक संग काज कऽ रहल अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय रेडक्रस आ रेड क्रिसेंट सोसाइटी महासंघ (आईएफआरसी) कहलक अछि जे ओ “गौण बाढ़िसँ बहुत, बहुत चिंतित अछि ।”

आईएफआरसी के मानना ​​छै कि कम स॑ कम ९३,००० लोगऽ क॑ प्रभावित करलऽ गेलऽ छै आरू ओकरा “बहुत जरूरत छै” ।

article Rescue personnel carry a person affected by flash floods at Devghat in Nepal's Nuwakot district on August 26, 2026. Massive flooding killed eight people in Nepal on August 26, as Chinese state media reported "major casualties" from a mudslide at a T Expand

The Brief Hundreds of people are dead or missing after catastrophic flooding near the Nepal-China border. Rescue teams are using helicopters to reach communities cut off by damaged roads and bridges. Aid groups are providing food, medicine and emergency supplies while seeking cash donations.



Humanitarian organizations are mobilizing to support survivors as rescue teams search for hundreds of people missing after catastrophic floods near the Nepal-China border.

Hundreds are dead or missing after a deadly torrent of water and mud several stories high swept through communities Wednesday following a glacier collapse.

The Nepalese army has been using helicopters to rescue people because so many roads and bridges have been washed out.

What they're saying:

Dan Hovey, vice president of emergency response at Direct Relief, which provides medicines and healthcare to disaster-struck areas, said his organization had already pre-positioned emergency supplies in Nepal for the upcoming monsoon season. That preparation has enabled Direct Relief to help quickly during these unexpected floods.

RELATED: Netflix documentary star Nirmal Purja among 10 climbers confirmed dead after Pakistan avalanche

"Nepal is a very disaster-prone country," he said. "On the disaster vulnerability indexes, it’s one of the highest – from earthquakes, floods, drought, wildfires."

Nepal Flood: 538 dead, 1,500 missing Nepal police said Friday morning that the country’s death toll had risen to 53 from 390 a day earlier with 1,500 people missing including 90 Americans.

Big picture view:

In addition to the medicines and supplies already in Nepal, Direct Relief was readying more shipments to send to Nepal Thursday, said Hovey, adding that new donations would allow the nonprofit to provide more support in the months to come.

"This is going to be a long recovery process," Hovey said.

Responding organizations say giving cash is currently most needed to provide local agencies and nonprofits flexible funding to continue their relief efforts.

Here are some organizations aiding those on the Nepal-China border, including U.S. groups responding on the ground.

Urgent relief efforts underway after Nepal flooding disaster At least 350 people died and 1,000 are still missing after a flooding disaster in Nepal. A glacier collapse is believed to be the cause. Tommaso Della Longa of the International Federation of the Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies details the relief efforts.

How you can help victims

What you can do:

All Hands & Hearts, the disaster recovery nonprofit, says it is currently providing emergency relief in Nepal, where it has worked since 2015 and plans to continue its work of rebuilding schools and homes.

Catholic Relief Services, the international humanitarian agency, has partnered with Caritas Nepal to provide aid and social services, while also working to deploy its own teams to help relief efforts.

Global Giving, the support nonprofit, has launched the Nepal Flood Relief Fund that it hopes will raise $1.5 million to provide flexible funding for search and rescue efforts and other emergency responses, as well as infrastructure rebuilding and other recovery projects.

RELATED: Two helicopter pilots killed in crash while battling Utah wildfire

Humanity & Inclusion, the international victim assistance nonprofit, says it is already distributing emergency supplies and providing rehabilitation support inside local hospitals.

Save the Children, the international nonprofit, says it is already delivering cooking kits, mosquito nets and blankets to 1,000 households in the region and coordinating with national and local authorities to determine how to scale its response.

World Central Kitchen, Chef Jose Andres’ humanitarian nonprofit, says it is already feeding those in the region through its local partners. It plans to activate its distribution network to bring more food to the affected area.

The Source: The Associated Press contributed to this report. Information for this story came from reports by The Associated Press and statements from humanitarian organizations including Direct Relief, All Hands & Hearts, Catholic Relief Services, GlobalGiving, Humanity & Inclusion, Save the Children and World Central Kitchen. This story was reported from Los Angeles.

full_article:
Rescue workers have resumed a search for hundreds of people still missing two days after catastrophic flash flooding hit the border between Nepal and China.

Their efforts were briefly put on hold on Friday after a lake formed by debris began overflowing, threatening areas already devastated by the disaster.

"We have received a notice saying that the lake has broken its banks," Narendra Pariyar, the most senior bureaucrat of the hard-hit Rasuwa district, told DW. "We can see that the level of water in the river is rising."

Residents in Nepal's border district of Rasuwa were seen fleeing up hillsides as they braced for a surge in river levels, Reuters reported.

Authorities later said the threat had eased but that they were closely monitoring the situation.

Meanwhile, Nepal said the death toll had risen to 579, up from 390 a day earlier. China has updated its earlier count of three to five deaths in Tibet.

More than 2,000 are still believed to be missing, including over 500 foreigners from more than 30 countries.

Nepal: WHO and Red Cross warn disaster is 'not over'

The International Red Cross estimated that over 93,000 people have been directly affected by the catastrophe and are in urgent need of humanitarian assistance.

"We're of course very concerned about a secondary flood," said spokesman David Fisher at a press briefing in Geneva, adding that Red Cross relief trucks had been blocked by the lake which formed following the landslide.

Kamal Kishore, Head of the United ​Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction, warned of further "cascading hazards that might unfold" and said: "The disaster is ⁠not ​yet completely over. It is still ​unfolding in some ways."

The World Health Organization (WHO) warned of the risk of disease in the wake of the disaster.

"Following a disaster of this scale, displacement, overcrowding ⁠and disruption ​to water, sanitation and health services can increase the risk of infectious diseases, including diarrhoea and respiratory illnesses," said spokesman Tarik ​Jasarevic.

Rescuers had to put their efforts on hold after an overflowing lake threatened to unleash more flooding Image: Niranjan Shrestha/AP Photo/picture alliance

What is the latest update from China?

Wednesday's disaster, triggered by a glacial collapse that sent rock and meltwater surging into rivers below, left a new danger in its wake: a barrier lake formed upstream by debris dams.

China's Ministry of Water Resources said the lake held roughly 2 million cubic meters of water as of Thursday and was expected to receive another 3 million cubic meters — equivalent to about 1,200 Olympic swimming pools — over the following three days, with peak flow expected around September 1.

Chinese national broadcaster CCTV said the lake's barrier sat more than 10 kilometers (6.2 miles) from Gyirong Port, the border crossing that was engulfed by the initial flood, and is at an elevation roughly 1,000 meters (3,280 feet) above it.

The country had mobilized an eight-member engineering team to survey the lake by air and build 3D models of the site. Engineer Chen Hanxiao described the difficulty of the terrain: "After the glacier collapse created the lake, many isolated cliffs and steep cliffs appeared along it," he told CCTV.

He said the team's general strategy was to dig a drainage channel at a lower point of the dam, though the channel's exact width and depth would depend on calculations of water flow and how quickly the lake continued to fill.

Their survey found the lake to be about 150 meters long and 40-50 meters deep. Continuing rain in the area, which is forecast to last through the coming week, has further destabilized the surrounding soil and rock.

On Friday afternoon, Chinese state media reported that the first professional rescue teams had reached the "core rescue site" or the area wiped out by a mudslide.

Hundreds of foreign tourists are among the missing Image: Navesh Chitrakar/REUTERS

What did Nepal say about search and rescue?

Nepal's Foreign Ministry said Friday it does not need foreign assistance for search-and-rescue operations, despite offers of help from several countries with nationals still missing.



Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lok Bahadur Chhetri said Nepal's security agencies were managing the response.



"The offer for help is natural. Our security agencies are doing the search and rescue operation. For now we don't require such help," he said.



Hundreds of foreign nationals remain unaccounted for, including from South Korea, which has already sent a response team and plans to dispatch a disaster relief unit. South Korea's Foreign Ministry confirmed that Nepal had indicated it was not yet ready to accept foreign rescue teams, adding, "South Korea will keep negotiating with Nepal over the matter."



Seoul has pledged $1 million (€860,000) in humanitarian aid through international organizations, after reporting nine of its nationals missing and 10 stranded after a hydropower plant they were working at was hit by the flood.



According to local media, India, China, the United States, Britain, Japan, South Korea, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh have all asked Nepal's government for permission to send their own search-and-rescue teams to assist.

Thirty-two Canadian citizens and permanent residents are among the nearly 2,000 people missing after the catastrophic flash flood along the Himalayan border between Nepal and Tibet, Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand confirmed Friday.

Anand confirmed during a media conference that 579 bodies had been recovered in the area so far and 1,924 people were still unaccounted for. Of those, 517 are foreign nationals, she said.

No Canadians are among those confirmed dead, Anand added.

"Nepal is facing a de vastating humanitarian emergency with catastrophic damage," she said.

Canada also announced it was providing $5 million to support emergency relief funds to Nepal.

Meanwhile, rescuers worked through mud and debris Friday in areas devastated by the flood, continuing the search for those still missing.

Nepalese and Chinese authorities also warned of further flooding from a lake that formed upstream after Wednesday's disaster and was already overflowing. They urged people in potentially affected areas to move to safer ground.

Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority says 3,742 people have been rescued.

The missing include tourists from several countries . Nepalese army spokesperson Brig.-Gen. Raja Ram Basnet told The Associated Press that a team had been deployed Friday to the Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project near the Nepal-China border following reports that people were trapped inside a tunnel.

"It is complicated to find the entry and exit points of the tunnel because everything has been covered by mud," Basnet said. "Our first priority is rescuing the stranded people."

The rescue effort has been challenging, and it's difficult to access some of the communities that have been most affected, Santosh Pandey, Oxfam's humanitarian lead in Nepal, told CBC's As it Happens from Kathmandu.

"Entire villages, entire communities, have been swept away. There is no one actually in the community to help each other," Pandey said.

"A lot of public infrastructure has been damaged, a lot of hospitals and health facilities have been completely swept away.

"It's a very chaotic situation right now."

Rescue workers climb through mud to free people trapped in tunnels 9 hours ago | Duration 0:29 Emergency responders rescued 350 people trapped inside a tunnel, shown in video released Nepal’s Prime Minister’s Office on Friday. Efforts are contuining to aid more than 100 people who are still trapped, after Wednesday’s flash flooding that destroyed villages and infrastructure in Nepal.

'We have to find him'

As rescuers work to reach remaining survivors, desperate families have crowded around hospitals trying to see if their loved ones can be identified among the hundreds of bodies that have been recovered.

At the Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital, relatives peer at grim images lining a wall outside the forensic identification unit.

The photos show the badly battered bodies of victims, including young children who had been pulled from the mud.

“I came here because I hope I find [my brother]. I will search until my last breath is gone,” said Nirmala Sapkota Koholi, 49, who lives in the city of Lalitpur, south of Kathmandu.

“I have to go everywhere, we have to find him.”

Nirmala Sapkota Koholi, 49, lives in the city of Lalitpur, south of Kathmandu. She's seen searching for pictures of her younger brother among photos lining a wall outside the forensic identification unit at the Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital in Kathmandu on Friday. (Angela Johnston/CBC)

Koholi told CBC News that her younger brother, Pradip Kumar Sapkota, was working as a driver with a group of pilgrims, including some from the United States and India. He had been on his phone with his daughter at 8:45 a.m. Wednesday. His daughter heard a loud boom and then the call suddenly cut off. They haven’t been able to reach him since.

Koholi has been to three hospitals and believes one of the victim photos could be her brother.

“He was a very good person. That is why God took him away.”

WATCH | Lake poses new flood threat: Lake formed from glacial debris poses new flood threat at Nepal-Tibet border 7 hours ago | Duration 15:09 A new lake formed from debris from the glacial collapse on Wednesday has began to overflow, Nepalese authorities say, posing a new flood risk for areas downstream.

Red Cross raises alarm about secondary flood

Red Cross officials, at a news conference in Switzerland, expressed concern about a secondary flood and said that the organization's rescue operations were temporarily halted after trucks with relief supplies were were blocked ⁠ by further flooding.

"We believe that at ​least 93,000 people have been ​affected and are in great need," said David Fisher, head of delegation for the International Federation ​of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies ⁠in Nepal.

Nepal's Foreign Ministry said on Friday that it appreciated the offers of help from several countries ‌with nationals missing amid the disaster but that it was able to manage the rescue efforts at present.

10 Toronto residents on a trek in Nepal unaccounted for after deadly flash floods: non-profit group

Flood survivors, including injured people, were taken to Kathmandu and other locations.

The affected areas are popular with hikers and for pilgrimages to religious sites.

Vishnuram Ramaswamy works at a private company in the southern Indian city of Puducherry and said that he last spoke to his mother and two sisters who were on pilgrimage to Mount Kailash on Wednesday morning at 9 a.m.

"This was the first time they had gone on this pilgrimage and it was something my mother always wanted to do," he said.

Survivor sees 'black storm'

Customs officer Karbir Gaire is among some of the survivors in Timure, the closest Nepalese village to the border with Tibet.

Gaire reached his office around 8 a.m. on Wednesday and was busy working on his computer when he first felt the ground shake.

"Right after the shake, I noticed a black storm coming towards us," he recalled from Kathmandu, where he is back with family. "We all immediately started running out, and within a few seconds, we were climbing uphill on the opposite side of our office building. I think those 10 or so seconds saved some of us."

The disaster started with a glacier collapse that sent ice and rock flowing downstream, and which registered as a magnitude-5.2 seismic event at the U.S. Geological Survey.

The science behind Nepal's catastrophic flash floods August 27 | Duration 2:03 An entire river valley along the Nepal border was wiped out in seconds — but local radar showed no rain, and it wasn't an earthquake. CBC meteorologist Johanna Wagstaffe breaks down how a massive glacier collapse triggered a violent inland tsunami, and why geologists warn this unfolding climate disaster isn't over yet.

Gaire doesn't remember exactly how many people were in the office when the disaster struck, but his 15 colleagues have gone missing.

"It was like a Hollywood movie scene. I don't call it a flood, it was a tsunami," he said.

Gaire described Timure as a vibrant place filled with government offices, hotels, cafes, banks, primary schools, tea shops and residential buildings, where more than 1,500 people were living.

title: At least 90 Americans missing in Nepal flood among 2,000 unaccounted for - The Guardian
description: At least 90 Americans missing in Nepal flood among 2,000 unaccounted for  The Guardian
publisher.title: The Guardian
full_article:
At least 90 Americans were still missing on Friday among almost 2,000 people unaccounted for following the catastrophic flash flood along the Nepal-Tibet border on Wednesday.

With the official death toll creeping towards 600 on Friday and expected to continue rising, there were survivors, victims and missing people from many nationalities.

“We can confirm that three American citizens have been safely rescued in Nepal. We are not aware of any US citizen deaths at this time,” the state department said on Thursday, USA Today reported. At least 90 Americans who were in the affected area remained unaccounted for.

The Guardian has approached the state department for additional comment.

Many of the Americans who are missing were on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, a sacred site in Tibet revered by several faiths, including Hinduism and Buddhism.

Twenty-two Americans returning from a pilgrimage hosted by the Isha Foundation, were among 80 foundation members not yet located, founder and spiritual leader Sadhguru Vasudev said in a statement on Thursday. The India-based spiritual organization has a US campus in Tennessee.

Leslie Crespi, a community liaison for the foundation’s US campus, said: “We had communication with the coordinator of the group at about 9.05am Nepalese time [Wednesday] saying that they had arrived there. And then by 9.14am is when this flash flood hit.”

Crespi described the trekkers as “like family”, adding that it was a “lifelong dream to go and be there” in Nepal for many of them.

Among the missing Americans is 45-year-old Venus Rajnikant Patel. His brother, Dennis, said Patel, who had recently moved from St Louis to Cincinnati, had been planning the pilgrimage for two years.

Patel’s friend Jolene Gosha said his hotel had been in the flood zone and “we’re just hoping, hoping, that by some chance he was able to climb his way out of it … I don’t want to give myself false hope because I know the reality is that he’s probably not with us.”

Meanwhile, the family of 72-year-old Jitendra Patel of Long Island in New York were still trying to reach him, his son Sunny Patel said.

Patel said his father called on Wednesday morning to say he had crossed into Tibet, and the family later realized he was in the flood zone.

“My heart sank,” Patel said, adding that he “didn’t think it was possible that my dad would be there at ‘ground zero’” of the flooding disaster.

The family is “maybe hopeful”, he said, but they have not heard from him and their WhatsApp messages remain unanswered. “It gets worse by every hour, obviously,” Patel added.

Also missing are Rekha and Rashi Shashidharan, a New York mother and 14-year-old daughter who were also on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash.

They had spent several days in Kathmandu acclimating to the altitude before traveling towards Tibet with a tour group, Shekhar Agrawal, Rekha’s brother, told CNN.

Agrawal last spoke to them around 7.30am local time on Wednesday before they planned to cross into Tibet. “After that, there was radio silence, nothing, no contact whatsoever,” Agrawal said, adding that he believed they may have still been at their hotel when the flood hit.

Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, said the US “stands ready to support the government of Nepal with needed humanitarian assistance”.

Meanwhile, the US embassy in Nepal said that the state department would “provide $500,000 (approximately 76m Nepali rupees) in assistance through a global grant to Catholic Relief Services, which will help flood-affected communities with emergency shelter and relief supplies, as well as water, sanitation, and hygiene support”.

Massive landslides and catastrophic flash floods have wreaked havoc at the Nepal-China border, destroying houses, wiping out bridges and killing at least 538 people since the landslide on August 26. Additionally, around 2,500 people are currently missing.

Now all eyes are on two newly-formed lakes, created by the landslide. One of the lakes began overflowing Friday, according to Chinese state broadcaster CCTV, posing a risk of landslides or flash flooding.

Video footage and satellite imagery shows the immense scale of the disaster in some of the areas hit hardest by the floods.

title: Virginia family with 4 relatives missing in the Nepal-China floods pleads for more rescue help - ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
description: Virginia family with 4 relatives missing in the Nepal-China floods pleads for more rescue help  ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
publisher.title: ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
full_article:
Mukti Patel has huddled with family and friends at her parents' Richmond, Virginia, home since her dad, sister and two other relatives went missing in the catastrophic flash floods along the Nepal-China border.

She knows the hotel they were staying in was swept away. But as she shared memories of them on Friday, she caught herself.

“I shouldn't talk in past tense yet,” she said. “We don’t know anything.”

As rescuers continued pulling survivors from the mud, family members of some of the more than 2,000 people missing in the disaster were still holding out hope — however dim — that their loved ones survived.

On a Zoom call Thursday night, some family members wanted to know if they could reach the site and whether a relative might be trapped inside an air pocket, said Sanket Pandey, managing director of Himalayan Glacier Adventure and Travel Company.

The tour group, which has an office in Baltimore, had organized a two-week excursion to the region with 40 guests and seven tour guides. All of them are now missing, Pandey said. Their families are desperate for any information.

“It’s really difficult to have nothing,” he said.

Patel's family was in the Himalayan Glacier group when the floods struck on Wednesday, killing hundreds of people and leaving more than 2,000 missing. About 90 Americans are among those unaccounted for, according to the U.S. State Department.

Patel, 27, said her dad, Umesh Kumar, 56, had wanted to make the trip for many years and traveled through India to Nepal, where he was joined by her sister, Akanksha, 32, and her sister’s husband, Ishan, 32.

Ishan’s mom, Shilpa, 59, was also on the trek. Ishan and Shilpa Patel have dual Canadian and U.S. citizenship while Umesh Kumar and Akanksha Patel are Canadian citizens, according to Mukti Patel.

Akanksha Patel is a psychiatrist who wants to break stigma around mental health problems, her sister said.

“Everything I’ve done in life has been off the blueprint of my sister,” Mukti Patel said between tears in a phone interview. “There’s no ounce of meanness in her.”

Her father is a joyous person who helped victims of the COVID-19 pandemic, and her brother-in-law, an orthopedic surgeon, has brought great happiness to her sister's life, she said.

Ishan Patel turned 32 on Wednesday, and the family called to wish him a happy birthday. That was their last contact.

Mukti Patel said she would like more countries to help the rescue and recovery efforts.

“I want my family to come home,” she said.

title: Catholic agencies respond to Nepal floods, as U.S. bishop calls for greater international aid - OSV News
description: Catholic agencies respond to Nepal floods, as U.S. bishop calls for greater international aid  OSV News
publisher.title: OSV News
full_article:
(OSV News) — A U.S. Catholic bishop is calling on the international community to step up aid after devastating torrents of water and mud raged along the Nepal-China border, killing more than 580 with over 1,900 still missing.

“As we learn more about the devastating flash floods in Nepal, I offer the prayers and solidarity of the Catholic community in the United States for our brothers and sisters impacted by this disaster,” said Bishop A. Elias Zaidan of the St. Louis-based Maronite Eparchy of Our Lady of Lebanon of Los Angeles in an Aug. 27 statement.

A dog lies at the site of the flash floods and mudslide, at Devighat, Nuwakot district, Nepal, Aug. 28, 2026. (OSV News photo/Francis Mascarenhas, Reuters)

The disaster was triggered by a glacial collapse in Nepal’s Langtang National Park shortly after 8:30 a.m. Aug. 26, according to the U.S. Geological Survey. Debris from the 5.2 magnitude event flowed more than 60 miles, resulting in “catastrophic impacts downstream” in communities along the Trishuli and Bhote Koshi Rivers, said the agency.

Hundreds of missing, including Americans

Among the missing are close to 670 individuals from some 32 nations, 65 of whom are from the U.S. Many are part of tour groups and Hindu pilgrimages.

Amid rescue efforts, the region is bracing for a possible secondary flooding due to ongoing rainfall, according to the United Nations’ World Meteorological Organization.

Matti Maya Tamang, 28, speaks with her son Zoyal Ghale, 8, who was airlifted from Rasuwa after being injured in the deadly flash floods and mudslide, two days after they were separated following the floods, inside a hospital in Kathmandu, Nepal, Aug. 28, 2026. Picture taken with a mobile phone. (OSV News/Ranup Shrestha, Reuters)

Speaking in his role as chair of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops’ Committee on International Justice and Peace, Bishop Zaidan said, “I exhort the international community to mobilize greater humanitarian assistance support for vulnerable families and communities in Nepal.”

The bishop also encouraged “long-term efforts to help affected communities rebuild their homes, livelihoods, and critical infrastructure.”

He said that Catholic Relief Services, the USCCB’s international humanitarian and development agency, is “closely monitoring the emergency.”

Extent of the destruction ‘beyond comprehension’

CRS — part of Caritas Internationalis, the Catholic Church’s global humanitarian network — is also “coordinating with Caritas Nepal and local partners to assess urgent needs and determine how best to support affected communities,” said Bishop Zaidan.

Caritas emergency aid coordinator Raju Pradhan told German Catholic news outlet KNA that “the extent of the destruction” from the flooding “is almost beyond comprehension.”

A drone view of a broken bridge and damaged houses after the flash floods and mudslide, at Devighat, Nuwakot district, Nepal, Aug. 28, 2026. (OSV News photo/Francis Mascarenhas, Reuters)

Disaster alerts the Nepalese government said it had issued “came too late” for those “near the source of the flood,” said Pradhan. “But further downstream, without these warnings, many more people would likely have lost their lives.”

Still, KNA reported, many did not fully grasp the urgency of those warnings.

Like CRS, Germany’s Freiburg-based Caritas is working with Caritas Nepal to provide assistance, including food, water, blankets and sleeping bags, as well as emergency shelters for kids and teens.

“In just one small town where we’ve been active for some time, 400 homes were destroyed,” said Pradhan, who also expressed concerns over the risk of secondary flooding.

Donations urgently needed

Pradhan stressed to KNA the need for long-term relief efforts in addressing the scope of the disaster — which “will require a lot of money, which we don’t have at the moment.”

CRS has set up an emergency relief fund in response to the flooding, with donations accepted by a number of online giving platforms, as well as phone and mail.

(OSV News photo/Toby Melville, Reuters)

In his statement, Bishop Zaidan expressed his gratitude for “the partnership of the U.S. government in supporting CRS’ essential work in these communities.”

He added, “We are also grateful to hear that the U.S. Department of State is closely monitoring the situation and deploying key personnel to support response efforts.”

Bishop Zaidan invoked Mary’s Immaculate Heart to “provide consolation and shelter to all those affected by this disaster.”

And, he said, “May she inspire the international community to work together, as one family, to address the urgent needs of the Nepalese people.”
